We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval and Consolidation in Large Language Models through Function Tokens
papers.research_question: How is memory retrieved during inference and consolidated during pre-training in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Function Token Hypothesis to explain memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs, where function tokens activate predictive features during inference and drive feature learning during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Function Token Hypothesis, which explains how function tokens drive memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
During inference, a small set of function tokens activate the majority of the model's features.
Function tokens dynamically reactivate the most predictive features from the context to guide next-token prediction.
During pre-training, the prediction of content tokens following function tokens dominates the loss and drives feature expansion.
Pre-training initially focuses on learning to predict function tokens before learning content tokens.
Scaling model size primarily enhances the prediction of content tokens.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain how function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
future_direction: How function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
How post-training modifies activation patterns in function tokens.
The dynamics of feature formation and the underlying reason for the scale-free property of token-feature activation.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) stems from their ability to consolidate vast amounts of knowledge into the memory during pre-training and to retrieve it from the memory during inference, enabling advanced capabilities such as knowledge memorization, instruction-following and reasoning. However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. We provide extensive experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis. Using bipartite graph analysis, we show that a small number of function tokens activate the majority of features. Case studies further reveal how function tokens activate the most predictive features from context to direct next token prediction. We also find that during pre-training, the training loss is dominated by predicting the next content tokens following function tokens, which forces the function tokens to select the most predictive features from context.

papers.title: Functional Abstraction of Knowledge Recall in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the knowledge recall mechanism in large language models be abstracted into a functional structure, and how can this perspective be used to improve knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a functional abstraction of knowledge recall in LLMs, showing that hidden activation vectors correspond to independent functional components (input, function body, return value). This perspective is used to improve contextual knowledge editing via activation patching.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge recall process in LLMs can be abstracted as a functional structure with localized activation vectors serving as independent components, and this abstraction enables more effective knowledge editing through activation patching.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-aware activation vectors are localized to specific token positions and layers: subject and relation vectors in early layers within their token ranges, object vectors in late layers at the final token.
These localized activation vectors function as independent components (input argument, function body, return value) in the knowledge recall process.
Activation interchange experiments show that subject, relation, and object vectors can be swapped independently, supporting the functional abstraction.
The proposed knowledge-scoring algorithm based on activation patching can accurately identify these functional components.
Applying this functional perspective via activation patching improves the efficacy of contextual knowledge editing prompts.
papers.limitation:
The proposed knowledge scoring algorithm relies on a brute-force search method, resulting in high time complexity.
The framework awaits validation on text-generation and general question-answering tasks that specifically involve knowledge recall.
The accuracy of the proposed knowledge editing method requires improvement, suggesting representation rewriting does not fully encapsulate the original knowledge.
future_direction: Developing more efficient knowledge exploration algorithms.
Validating the framework on text-generation and general question-answering tasks.
Deeper exploration of the knowledge storage mechanisms within LLMs.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained transformer large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong knowledge recall capabilities. This paper investigates the knowledge recall mechanism in LLMs by abstracting it into a functional structure. We propose that during knowledge recall, the model's hidden activation space implicitly entails a function execution process where specific activation vectors align with functional components (Input argument, Function body, and Return values). Specifically, activation vectors of relation-related tokens define a mapping function from subjects to objects, with subject-related token activations serving as input arguments and object-related token activations as return values. For experimental verification, we first design a patching-based knowledge-scoring algorithm to identify knowledge-aware activation vectors as independent functional components. Then, we conduct counter-knowledge testing to examine the independent functional effects of each component on knowledge recall outcomes. From this functional perspective, we improve the contextual knowledge editing approach augmented by activation patching. By rewriting incoherent activations in context, we enable improved short-term memory retention for new knowledge prompting.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: On Large Language Models' Hallucination with Regard to Known Facts
papers.research_question: Why do large language models hallucinate on known facts, and how can we detect such hallucinations by analyzing inference dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that hallucinations on known facts arise from failed knowledge recall, and that the dynamics of output token probabilities across layers differ between correct and hallucinated cases. These dynamic patterns can be used as features to build a classifier that detects hallucinations with high accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The cause of hallucinations lies in the failure of factual recall, potentially due to biased subject parsing and inadequate object information extraction. The dynamic patterns in reasoning can be used to detect hallucinations, offering a novel perspective for analyzing model outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Known fact hallucination arises from failed knowledge recall, with correct answers appearing in top ranks less frequently during inference compared to correct outputs.
MLP modules have a more significant impact on incorrect outputs than attention modules, suppressing correct information and contributing to erroneous outputs.
In hallucinated cases, the output token's information rarely shows abrupt increases and consistent superiority in later layers, unlike correct cases.
The dynamic patterns of output token probabilities across layers can be used as features for hallucination detection.
A classifier using these dynamic patterns achieves an 88% success rate in detecting hallucinatory predictions.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies on triplet knowledge datasets, potentially limiting generalizability to other knowledge structures or domains.
The study primarily focused on a single transformer model (llama2-7b-chat), and future research should encompass a broader spectrum of models.
The study offers a preliminary understanding, and comprehensive elucidation of internal state variations and their influence on output remains complex and requires deeper investigation.
future_direction: Explore the impact of query formulation on known knowledge recall and methods to mitigate such hallucinations.
Generalize the perspective to broader forms of knowledge outputs and more complex reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models are successful in answering factoid questions but are also prone to hallucination. We investigate the phenomenon of LLMs possessing correct answer knowledge yet still hallucinating from the perspective of inference dynamics, an area not previously covered in studies on hallucinations. We are able to conduct this analysis via two key ideas. First, we identify the factual questions that query the same triplet knowledge but result in different answers. The difference between the model behaviors on the correct and incorrect outputs hence suggests the patterns when hallucinations happen. Second, to measure the pattern, we utilize mappings from the residual streams to vocabulary space. We reveal the different dynamics of the output token probabilities along the depths of layers between the correct and hallucinated cases. In hallucinated cases, the output token's information rarely demonstrates abrupt increases and consistent superiority in the later stages of the model. Leveraging the dynamic curve as a feature, we build a classifier capable of accurately detecting hallucinatory predictions with an 88\% success rate. Our study shed light on understanding the reasons for LLMs' hallucinations on their known facts, and more importantly, on accurately predicting when they are hallucinating.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: RECALL: Library-Like Behavior In Language Models is Enhanced by Self-Referencing Causal Cycles
papers.research_question: How can self-referencing causal cycles (RECALL) mitigate the reversal curse in autoregressive language models, enabling them to recall preceding context from succeeding tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces self-referencing causal cycles (RECALL) as a natural mechanism in pretraining data that enables autoregressive language models to bypass the reversal curse, and proposes a two-step prompting strategy to leverage it for reliable information retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Self-referencing causal cycles (RECALL) provide a natural mechanism for language models to overcome the reversal curse, and leveraging these cycles through prompting can improve the reliability of responses to prompts affected by the curse.
papers.key_findings:
RECALL enables models to recall preceding tokens from succeeding ones through cycle tokens, which create self-referencing causal cycles.
Cycle tokens act as hyperlinks in pretraining data, allowing models to bridge distant parts of text.
A two-step RECALL-aware prompting strategy (recollect context, then utilize it) effectively resolves the preceding line problem in key writings.
RECALL works under stochastic conditions with candidate sets, with accuracy inversely proportional to candidate set size.
The reversal curse can be mitigated without architectural changes or data augmentation by leveraging naturally occurring cycles.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted in controlled settings with simplified token sequences.
Real-world performance may be influenced by additional factors such as retrieval-augmented generation or web search.
Further interpretability techniques may be required to precisely attribute parametric information retrieval to specific cycle tokens.
Larger models often utilize fully or partially closed-source training data, making extraction of pretraining data difficult.
papers.abstract: We introduce the concept of the self-referencing causal cycle (abbreviated RECALL) - a mechanism that enables large language models (LLMs) to bypass the limitations of unidirectional causality, which underlies a phenomenon known as the reversal curse. When an LLM is prompted with sequential data, it often fails to recall preceding context. For example, when we ask an LLM to recall the line preceding "O say does that star-spangled banner yet wave" in the U.S. National Anthem, it often fails to correctly return "Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there" - this is due to the reversal curse. It occurs because language models such as ChatGPT and Llama generate text based on preceding tokens, requiring facts to be learned and reproduced in a consistent token order. While the reversal curse is often viewed as a limitation, we offer evidence of an alternative view: it is not always an obstacle in practice. We find that RECALL is driven by what we designate as cycle tokens - sequences that connect different parts of the training data, enabling recall of preceding tokens from succeeding ones. Through rigorous probabilistic formalization and controlled experiments, we demonstrate how the cycles they induce influence a model's ability to reproduce information. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide our code and experimental details at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/remember-B0B8/.

papers.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: (I) Linear Separability: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; (II) Depth Localization: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; (III) Hierarchical Consistency: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and (IV) Directional Asymmetry: reinforcing the model's implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures.

papers.title: Understanding Verbatim Memorization in LLMs Through Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: What specific circuits in the model are responsible for initiating and maintaining verbatim memorization, and how do they differ from non-memorized generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive datasets and circuit discovery to identify circuits responsible for memorization in LLMs, finding that initiation circuits can also maintain memorization, but maintenance circuits cannot initiate it, and that memorization prevention transfers across domains while induction is context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that memorization initiation and maintenance are handled by different circuits, with initiation circuits being more general and maintenance circuits being more specific. Memorization prevention transfers across domains, while induction is context-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Created two distinct contrastive datasets for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks.
Discovered compact circuits (≤5% of model edges) for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks using attribution patching techniques.
Circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.
Memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains (GitHub, Enron Emails, Common Crawl), while memorization induction appears more context-dependent.
Removing memorization (noising approach) is easier than inducing memorization (denoising approach) in the studied setup.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG) for circuit discovery, which provides only an approximation and may not fully correlate with direct activation patching measurements.
Findings are limited to a single, relatively small language model (GPT-Neo-125m); larger models might employ more complex or differently distributed memorization mechanisms.
Uncertainty about whether the identified circuits represent general memorization mechanisms or are specific to the Wikipedia subset of The Pile or artifacts of the contrastive dataset construction.
future_direction: Investigate how memorization mechanisms scale with model size.
Explore whether similar circuits exist in different model architectures.
Expand testing to more diverse datasets and memorization criteria to establish the generality of these mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Underlying mechanisms of memorization in LLMs-the verbatim reproduction of training data-remain poorly understood.What exact part of the network decides to retrieve a token that we would consider as start of memorization sequence?How exactly is the models' behaviour different when producing memorized sentence vs non-memorized?In this work we approach these questions from mechanistic interpretability standpoint by utilizing transformer circuits-the minimal computational subgraphs that perform specific functions within the model.Through carefully constructed contrastive datasets, we identify points where model generation diverges from memorized content and isolate the specific circuits responsible for two distinct aspects of memorization.We find that circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.Intriguingly, memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains, while memorization induction appears more contextdependent. 1

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: Token Erasure as a Footprint of Implicit Vocabulary Items in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs convert arbitrary groups of tokens into useful higher-level representations, specifically through the mechanism of token erasure in early layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that last token representations of multi-token words and entities exhibit token erasure in early layers, and proposes a method based on this effect to extract the implicit vocabulary of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: This work presents preliminary evidence for the existence of an implicit vocabulary in LLMs and introduces a method to probe it, serving as a first step towards understanding lexical representation formation.
papers.key_findings:
Last token positions of multi-token words and named entities show token erasure in early layers for both Llama-2-7b and Llama-3-8b.
The erasure effect is consistent across different datasets, including COUNTERFACT and Wikipedia.
A heuristic erasure score ψ is developed to identify lexical items by measuring drops in token prediction probability between layers.
The method can read out implicit vocabulary items, recovering sequences like multi-token words, entities, and expressions, with differences observed between models due to token vocabulary size.
The implicit vocabulary includes non-compositional lexical items such as multi-token words, named entities, and idiomatic expressions.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation of implicit vocabulary-building methods is challenging due to the lack of a known ground-truth.
Analysis is restricted to known entities, and it is unclear how the method applies to intermediate cases like fictional names or less famous people.
Measurements have been run only on the Llama family of models and do not extend to non-Llama models or larger Llama models.
papers.abstract: LLMs process text as sequences of tokens that roughly correspond to words, where less common words are represented by multiple tokens. However, individual tokens are often semantically unrelated to the meanings of the words/concepts they comprise. For example, Llama-2-7b's tokenizer splits the word "northeastern" into the tokens ['_n', 'ort', 'he', 'astern'], none of which correspond to semantically meaningful units like "north" or "east." Similarly, the overall meanings of named entities like "Neil Young" and multi-word expressions like "break a leg" cannot be directly inferred from their constituent tokens. Mechanistically, how do LLMs convert such arbitrary groups of tokens into useful higher-level representations? In this work, we find that last token representations of named entities and multi-token words exhibit a pronounced "erasure" effect, where information about previous and current tokens is rapidly forgotten in early layers. Using this observation, we propose a method to "read out" the implicit vocabulary of an autoregressive LLM by examining differences in token representations across layers, and present results of this method for Llama-2-7b and Llama-3-8B. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to probe the implicit vocabulary of an LLM.

papers.title: Say Anything but This: When Tokenizer Betrays Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does tokenization, specifically non-unique token ID mappings, contribute to reasoning failures in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a non-trivial fraction of reasoning failures in LLMs stems from the tokenizer's non-injective mapping between token ID sequences and surface strings, leading to 'phantom edits' where models change token IDs but output identical text.
papers.conclusion: Tokenizer-induced representational mismatches cause reasoning failures in LLMs, and scaling alone cannot resolve these deficiencies, motivating tokenizer-level remedies and more robust representational schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Tokenization non-uniqueness leads to 'phantom edits' where models output different token IDs for a target word while the decoded surface text remains identical.
A taxonomy of eight systematic tokenizer artifacts (e.g., whitespace-boundary shifts, intra-word resegmentation) is identified as the mechanisms behind these failures.
Model scaling does not eliminate these failures; they persist across model families and parameter sizes.
A token-ID masking intervention reduces phantom edits, indicating models possess the underlying reasoning capacity but are misled by tokenizer artifacts.
Most phantom edits (72.2%) preserve subtoken count (1→1 transitions) and are primarily due to whitespace-variant token pairs.
papers.limitation: The token-ID masking intervention is a post-hoc, superficial remedy that does not address the fundamental many-to-one mapping property of tokenization, and complete tokenizer redesign and model re-training remain computationally expensive.
future_direction: Test whether tokenization non-uniqueness affects reasoning behaviors beyond the replacement probe, such as chain-of-thought stability or multi-step arithmetic accuracy.
Develop tokenizer-aware training objectives that enforce representational consistency across equivalent encodings.
Redesign tokenizers to shrink equivalence classes, for example by eliminating duplicate forms of the same word.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reason over discrete token ID sequences, yet modern subword tokenizers routinely produce non-unique encodings: multiple token ID sequences can detokenize to identical surface strings. This representational mismatch creates an unmeasured fragility wherein reasoning processes can fail. LLMs may treat two internal representations as distinct "words" even when they are semantically identical at the text level. In this work, we show that tokenization can betray LLM reasoning through one-to-many token ID mappings. We introduce a tokenization-consistency probe that requires models to replace designated target words in context while leaving all other content unchanged. The task is intentionally simple at the surface level, enabling us to attribute failures to tokenizer-detokenizer artifacts rather than to knowledge gaps or parameter limitations. Through analysis of over 11000 replacement trials across state-of-the-art open-source LLMs, we find a non-trivial rate of outputs exhibit phantom edits: cases where models operate under the illusion of correct reasoning, a phenomenon arising from tokenizer-induced representational defects. We further analyze these cases and provide a taxonomy of eight systematic tokenizer artifacts, including whitespace-boundary shifts and intra-word resegmentation. These findings indicate that part of apparent reasoning deficiency originates in the tokenizer layer, motivating tokenizer-level remedies before incurring the cost of training ever-larger models on ever-larger corpora.

papers.title: On the Representations of Entities in Auto-regressive Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally represent named entities, and can we decode entity mentions from these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Entity Lens, a method for decoding multi-token entity mentions from internal representations, and provides evidence that LLMs develop specialized mechanisms for representing and manipulating entities.
papers.conclusion: The results support the existence of an entity representation space within LLMs, paving the way for more explainable and controllable language models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can decode entity mentions from last token representations, with performance depending on entity frequency rather than token length.
Average representations and linearly cleaned representations improve decoding performance compared to last token representations.
In contextual decoding, LLMs can reliably detect and copy entity mentions from context, achieving near-optimal performance.
Entity representations can be linearly transformed to decode basic relations between entities.
The Entity Lens visualizes which entity the model associates with a given representation at any layer.
papers.limitation:
Task vectors are layer-specific and assume layer-agnostic representations, which may not fully hold.
Entity Lens currently generates only a single mention and does not provide top-k mappings like the traditional logit lens.
future_direction: Developing a generalist task vector that works across layers.
Extending Entity Lens to generate top-k mentions via beam-search.
papers.abstract: Named entities are fundamental building blocks of knowledge in text, grounding factual information and structuring relationships within language. Despite their importance, it remains unclear how Large Language Models (LLMs) internally represent entities. Prior research has primarily examined explicit relationships, but little is known about entity representations themselves. We introduce entity mention reconstruction as a novel framework for studying how LLMs encode and manipulate entities. We investigate whether entity mentions can be generated from internal representations, how multi-token entities are encoded beyond last-token embeddings, and whether these representations capture relational knowledge. Our proposed method, leveraging _task vectors_, allows to consistently generate multi-token mentions from various entity representations derived from the LLMs hidden states. We thus introduce the _Entity Lens_, extending the _logit-lens_ to predict multi-token mentions. Our results bring new evidence that LLMs develop entity-specific mechanisms to represent and manipulate any multi-token entities, including those unseen during training. Our code is avalable at https://github.com/VictorMorand/EntityRepresentations .

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: Exposing Attention Glitches with Flip-Flop Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The paper investigates the phenomenon of attention glitches as a potential cause.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of attention glitches in Transformers, introduces flip-flop language modeling (FFLM) as a synthetic benchmark to isolate these errors, and finds that Transformers exhibit a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors even on this simple task.
papers.conclusion: Attention glitches are a fundamental failure mode of Transformer architectures when processing long-range dependencies, and may account for some closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit a long, irregular tail of reasoning errors (attention glitches) on flip-flop language modeling, while LSTMs extrapolate perfectly.
Natural language models (e.g., GPT-4, Pythia) can process flip-flop languages but not robustly, with error rates amplifying with sequence length.
Training on out-of-distribution data (rare sequences) significantly reduces errors, more so than scaling model size or training data.
Attention-sharpening regularizers reduce reasoning errors by an order of magnitude by promoting sparse attention patterns.
No mitigation tried (including regularization, architecture changes, and scaling) completely eliminated attention glitches.
papers.limitation:
None of the attempted mitigations (regularization, architecture changes, scaling) were successful in driving the number of errors to exactly zero.
Attention patterns may not be fully reliable for interpretability, as they can interact with other components in non-intuitive ways.
future_direction: A more thorough study of the training dynamics of flip-flop tasks with attention-sharpening regularization.
Understanding how to build robust Transformer models and training pipelines at larger scales.
Investigating the connection between attention glitches and closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models.
papers.abstract: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The brittleness of these models, particularly when executing long chains of reasoning, currently seems to be an inevitable price to pay for their advanced capabilities of coherently synthesizing knowledge, pragmatics, and abstract thought. Towards making sense of this fundamentally unsolved problem, this work identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of attention glitches, in which the Transformer architecture's inductive biases intermittently fail to capture robust reasoning. To isolate the issue, we introduce flip-flop language modeling (FFLM), a parametric family of synthetic benchmarks designed to probe the extrapolative behavior of neural language models. This simple generative task requires a model to copy binary symbols over long-range dependencies, ignoring the tokens in between. We find that Transformer FFLMs suffer from a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors, some of which we can eliminate using various regularization techniques. Our preliminary mechanistic analyses show why the remaining errors may be very difficult to diagnose and resolve. We hypothesize that attention glitches account for (some of) the closed-domain hallucinations in natural LLMs.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Guess or Recall? Training CNNs to Classify and Localize Memorization in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the existing taxonomy of memorized samples align with distinct attention mechanisms? What taxonomy best captures the attention mechanisms involved in memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to analyze memorization in LLMs by training CNNs on attention weights, and introduces a new taxonomy (Guess, Recall, Non-memorized) that better captures distinct attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed taxonomy and method show that memorization mechanisms can be distinguished via attention weights, with Guess and Recall relying on different layers, and few-shot memorization is not a distinct category.
papers.key_findings:
The existing taxonomy (Prashanth et al. 2024) aligns poorly with attention weights (64.7% F1).
Few-shot verbatim memorization does not correspond to a distinct attention mechanism.
A significant proportion of extractable samples are guessed (using language modeling) rather than recalled.
The new taxonomy (Guess, Recall, Non-memorized) aligns well with attention weights (89.0% F1).
Guess samples rely on lower layers, while Recall samples rely on short-range interactions in upper layers.
papers.abstract: Verbatim memorization in Large Language Models (LLMs) is a multifaceted phenomenon involving distinct underlying mechanisms. We introduce a novel method to analyze the different forms of memorization described by the existing taxonomy. Specifically, we train Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on the attention weights of the LLM and evaluate the alignment between this taxonomy and the attention weights involved in decoding. We find that the existing taxonomy performs poorly and fails to reflect distinct mechanisms within the attention blocks. We propose a new taxonomy that maximizes alignment with the attention weights, consisting of three categories: memorized samples that are guessed using language modeling abilities, memorized samples that are recalled due to high duplication in the training set, and non-memorized samples. Our results reveal that few-shot verbatim memorization does not correspond to a distinct attention mechanism. We also show that a significant proportion of extractable samples are in fact guessed by the model and should therefore be studied separately. Finally, we develop a custom visual interpretability technique to localize the regions of the attention weights involved in each form of memorization.

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Can VLMs Recall Factual Associations From Visual References?
papers.research_question: Do VLMs have a systematic deficiency in recalling factual associations from visual references compared to textual references?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs exhibit a systematic deficiency in recalling factual knowledge from visual references compared to textual references, and this failure can be detected with high accuracy using linear probes on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: VLMs have a multimodal grounding gap that makes them struggle to link visual representations to internal knowledge, and probes on hidden states can help identify such failures; addressing this gap is important for future research.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs show a significant performance drop (over 50% on average) when forced to rely on visual references compared to textual references for factual recall.
This grounding gap persists across different model families, scales, and datasets.
Hidden state patterns differ between successful and failed linking cases, with failures building confidence later in the network.
Linear probes on hidden states can detect linking failures with over 92% accuracy and generalize to out-of-domain datasets.
Using these probes for selective prediction increases coverage by 7.87% and reduces error risk by 0.9% on OKVQA.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses exclusively on VLMs, leaving open whether similar gaps exist in other multimodal LMs (e.g., audio language models).
The paper does not address mitigating linking failure during VLM training.
The paper does not identify which particular design decision leads to the grounding gap.
future_direction: Expand feature-alignment pretraining to include factual recall tasks to improve grounding.
Investigate the grounding gap in other multimodal LMs (e.g., audio language models).
Identify which particular design decision leads to the grounding gap.
papers.abstract: Through a controlled study, we identify a systematic deficiency in the multimodal grounding of Vision Language Models (VLMs). While VLMs can recall factual associations when provided a textual reference to an entity; their ability to do so is significantly diminished when the reference is visual instead. Forcing VLMs to rely on image representations of an entity halves their ability to recall factual knowledge, suggesting that VLMs struggle to link their internal knowledge of an entity with its image representation. We show that such linking failures are correlated with the expression of distinct patterns in model internal states, and that probes on these internal states achieve over 92% accuracy at flagging cases where the VLM response is unreliable. These probes can be applied, without retraining, to identify when a VLM will fail to correctly answer a question that requires an understanding of multimodal input. When used to facilitate selective prediction on a visual question answering task, the probes increase coverage by 7.87% (absolute) while also reducing the risk of error by 0.9% (absolute). Addressing the systematic, detectable deficiency is an important avenue in language grounding, and we provide informed recommendations for future directions.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Model Non-Factual Hallucinations
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanistic causes of non-factual hallucinations in language models, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies two mechanistic causes of non-factual hallucinations in LMs—knowledge enrichment failures in lower MLPs and answer extraction failures in upper attention heads—and proposes a mitigation method based on restoring the internal fact recall pipeline.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that abnormal operation of lower MLPs and upper attention heads leads to distinct hallucination mechanisms, and introduces an effective mitigation method based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations are caused by two distinct mechanisms: knowledge enrichment failures in lower layer MLPs and answer extraction failures in upper layer attention heads.
These mechanisms have different external manifestations, such as subject-object association strengths and robustness to input perturbations.
The proposed MHM method effectively mitigates hallucinations by targeting both MLP and attention components during fine-tuning.
MHM outperforms baselines like SFT, ICL, MEND, and DoLa on open-domain QA datasets.
The findings are consistent across multiple LMs including Llama-2, Pythia, and GPT-J.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on logit lens for interpreting intermediate layers, which only approximates encoded information.
Focus on simple input sequences may not capture real-world LM behavior with complex contexts.
future_direction: Use more sophisticated methods like Tuned Lens to probe layer information.
Apply mechanistic interpretability to more complex and naturalistic contexts.
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art language models (LMs) sometimes generate non-factual hallucinations that misalign with world knowledge. To explore the mechanistic causes of these hallucinations, we create diagnostic datasets with subject-relation queries and adapt interpretability methods to trace hallucinations through internal model representations. We discover two general and distinct mechanistic causes of hallucinations shared across LMs (Llama-2, Pythia, GPT-J): 1) knowledge enrichment hallucinations: insufficient subject attribute knowledge in lower layer MLPs, and 2) answer extraction hallucinations: failure to select the correct object attribute in upper layer attention heads. We also found these two internal mechanistic causes of hallucinations are reflected in external manifestations. Based on insights from our mechanistic analysis, we propose a novel hallucination mitigation method through targeted restoration of the LM's internal fact recall pipeline, demonstrating superior performance compared to baselines.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
